questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is given a cholinergic agonist during a study of autonomic reflexes, and his heart rate slows. Activation of which of the following signaling pathways in cardiac tissue is most directly responsible for this effect?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gq-coupled receptor that increases IP3 and intracellular calcium

explanation.summary: Cardiac slowing by cholinergics is mediated by the M2 receptor, a Gi-coupled GPCR that lowers cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the heart, muscarinic M2 receptors couple to Gi, decreasing cAMP and reducing rate and AV nodal conduction. This is why parasympathetic (cholinergic) activation slows the pulse.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gq with increased IP3/Ca2+ is the M1/M3 pathway for glands and smooth muscle, not the cardiac slowing pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gs increases cAMP and would raise, not lower, heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ligand-gated Na+/K+ channels describe nicotinic (Nm) receptors at the neuromuscular junction, not cardiac muscarinic signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic receptors are GPCRs, not tyrosine kinase receptors.

questions.stem: Which muscarinic receptor subtype is primarily responsible for slowing the heart rate and impulse conduction through the cardiac nodes?

explanation.summary: The M2 receptor mediates cholinergic slowing of the heart.
explanation.whyCorrect: M2 is the dominant cardiac muscarinic receptor; via Gi it decreases cAMP and slows the pulse rate and conduction through the SA and AV nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M1 is a Gq neuronal receptor associated with cognition, memory, and learning.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M3 is a Gq receptor driving gland secretion and smooth-muscle contraction, not cardiac slowing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M5 is not the clinically important cardiac subtype; M1-M3 are the key clinical receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nm is the nicotinic ligand-gated channel at skeletal muscle, unrelated to nodal slowing.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man cannot void on the third postoperative day. There is no mechanical obstruction, and his bladder is markedly distended. A drug is chosen that contracts the detrusor muscle and relaxes the internal urethral sphincter to promote emptying. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

explanation.summary: Bethanechol is the direct-acting cholinergic used to treat non-obstructive urinary retention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bethanechol is an orally administered choline ester that causes bladder detrusor contraction and relaxes the urinary sphincter, treating urinary retention (and also ileus).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase and is not used therapeutically for retention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atropine is an antimuscarinic; it relaxes the detrusor and would worsen retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbachol is used ophthalmically for glaucoma, not for bladder emptying.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine is used for xerostomia and glaucoma, not urinary retention.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome has severe dry mouth that is also worse after prior head and neck radiation. She is started on an oral agent that stimulates salivary secretion. Which of the following was most likely prescribed?

explanation.summary: Pilocarpine is used orally to treat xerostomia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pilocarpine, a tertiary-amine alkaloid, is used for xerostomia after head and neck radiation and in Sjogren syndrome, where disrupted lacrimal and salivary function improves with cholinergic stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is an antimuscarinic that would reduce secretions and worsen dry mouth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bethanechol is used for urinary retention and ileus, not xerostomia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbachol is used as ophthalmic drops for glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methacholine is a diagnostic bronchoprovocation agent with no other therapeutic use.

questions.stem: A patient with glaucoma is treated with cholinergic eye drops. The reduction in intraocular pressure is best explained by which of the following drug-induced effects?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxation of the bladder detrusor muscle

explanation.summary: Cholinergic drops lower intraocular pressure by contracting the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbachol and pilocarpine cause miosis by contracting the pupillary sphincter and adjust the ciliary muscle, reducing resistance to aqueous humor outflow and thereby lowering intraocular pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergics cause bronchoconstriction, not bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholinergics increase, not decrease, lacrimal secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergics cause miosis, not mydriasis; mydriasis is an antimuscarinic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bladder effects are unrelated to the ocular mechanism of pressure reduction.

questions.stem: Indirect-acting cholinomimetic agents increase parasympathetic activity through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antagonizing nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking reuptake of norepinephrine at the synapse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directly binding and activating muscarinic receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing synthesis of choline in the presynaptic neuron

explanation.summary: Indirect-acting cholinomimetics are cholinesterase inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike direct-acting agents that bind receptors, indirect-acting cholinomimetics inhibit acetylcholinesterase, preventing breakdown of ACh and thereby increasing PNS activation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antagonizing nicotinic receptors would reduce, not increase, cholinergic transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking norepinephrine reuptake is an adrenergic action unrelated to cholinergic breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That describes direct-acting cholinomimetics, not the indirect class.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing choline synthesis is not the defined mechanism of these drugs.

questions.stem: Compared with acetylcholine, choline ester drugs such as carbachol have a longer duration of action. Which of the following properties best explains this difference?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible covalent binding to the receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid renal excretion of the active drug

explanation.summary: Choline esters are longer-acting because they resist acetylcholinesterase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Modification of the choline side chain makes esters like carbachol more resistant to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase than ACh, giving a longer duration of action. Methacholine is the exception, being rapidly hydrolyzed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These drugs do bind and activate muscarinic receptors, which is required for their effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Their action is receptor activation, not irreversible covalent binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rapid hydrolysis would shorten, not lengthen, duration; this describes ACh (and methacholine).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Duration is explained by enzymatic resistance, not renal excretion in this brick.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with intermittent cough and suspected asthma undergoes pulmonary function testing. An inhaled agent is administered to provoke bronchoconstriction as a diagnostic challenge. Which of the following was most likely used?

explanation.summary: Methacholine is used for bronchoprovocation testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methacholine is indicated for testing bronchospastic (bronchoprovocation) activity as a diagnostic tool and, unlike the other choline esters, is rapidly hydrolyzed and has no other therapeutic use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is an antimuscarinic and would block, not provoke, bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bethanechol is used for urinary retention and ileus, not bronchial testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbachol is an ophthalmic agent for glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine is used for xerostomia and glaucoma.

questions.stem: Activation of muscarinic receptors in the gastrointestinal tract produces which of the following effects?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contraction of the internal anal sphincter

explanation.summary: Cholinergic activation increases GI motility and secretions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscarinic (M3) activation increases gastric motility and secretions and relaxes the internal anal sphincter; the increased motility can cause diarrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased motility, not decreased, is the cholinergic effect, so constipation is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The internal anal sphincter relaxes rather than contracts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastric secretions increase with cholinergic activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salivation increases with cholinergic activation.

questions.stem: Cholinergic activation of the eye produces which of the following effects?

explanation.summary: Cholinergic activation of the eye causes miosis and ciliary contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscarinic activation contracts the sphincter and ciliary muscles of the eye, producing miosis (pupil constriction) and increased lacrimation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergic activation increases lacrimation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergic drugs lower intraocular pressure, which is why they treat glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mydriasis is an antimuscarinic effect, the opposite of cholinergic action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pupillary sphincter contracts, not relaxes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome is treated with oral pilocarpine. Which of the following adverse effects is she most likely to report, occurring in roughly half of patients?

explanation.summary: Pilocarpine commonly causes excessive sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pilocarpine is associated with excess sweating; about 50-60% of patients report this adverse effect due to cholinergic stimulation of sweat glands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergics increase GI motility and tend toward diarrhea, not constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergics increase secretions and sweating, so dry skin is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergics cause miosis, not mydriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic activation slows the heart, producing bradycardia rather than tachycardia.

questions.stem: Pilocarpine differs from choline ester cholinergics in that it is a tertiary-amine alkaloid. Which of the following properties does this structure confer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can only be administered intravenously

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is able to cross the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is rapidly degraded by acetylcholinesterase

explanation.summary: As a tertiary-amine alkaloid, pilocarpine crosses the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that pilocarpine is a tertiary amine that does cross the blood-brain barrier, distinguishing it from the choline esters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pilocarpine is given orally and ophthalmically, not only IV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist and does activate these receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its alkaloid structure is not a substrate rapidly cleaved by acetylcholinesterase like ACh.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine acts on muscarinic receptors, not selectively on nicotinic receptors.

questions.stem: A pharmacologist is describing how a class of drugs produces its effects. The drugs bind muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the peripheral nervous system and CNS but leave nicotinic receptors unaffected, and their actions are opposite to those of the rest-and-digest parasympathetic system. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of these drugs?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics (antimuscarinics) act by competitive inhibition of muscarinic receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that anticholinergics act primarily through competitive inhibition of muscarinic receptors in the PNS, CNS, or both, and that most do not block nicotinic receptors. Their effects are therefore opposite to those of parasympathetic (cholinergic) stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticholinergics target muscarinic, not adrenergic, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They antagonize rather than activate muscarinic receptors; agonism would produce cholinergic (parasympathetic) effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase raises acetylcholine and produces cholinergic effects, the opposite of an anticholinergic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticholinergics generally do not block nicotinic receptors, and their muscarinic blockade is competitive and reversible.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man in the emergency department has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with a heart rate of 38/min and lightheadedness. He is given intravenous atropine, and his heart rate rises to 74/min. Blockade of which receptor best explains this increase in heart rate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on the heart

choices.label: B
choices.text: M2 muscarinic receptors on the heart

choices.label: C
choices.text: M3 muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: M3 muscarinic receptors on glandular tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

explanation.summary: Atropine speeds the heart by blocking cardiac M2 muscarinic receptors, removing vagal slowing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's organ table lists the heart's effect as increased heart rate mediated by M2 receptors. Anticholinergics inhibit the parasympathetic (vagal) slowing of the heart, producing tachycardia, which is why atropine is useful in symptomatic bradycardia and AV node block.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist and does not act on beta-1 adrenergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Airway M3 receptors govern bronchial tone, not cardiac rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M3 receptors on glands mediate secretions (dry mouth), not heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuromuscular nicotinic receptors control skeletal muscle, not the heart rate, and are not blocked by atropine.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is planning a week-long ocean cruise and reports severe seasickness on prior trips. Her physician prescribes a transdermal patch that must be replaced after 72 hours. Which anticholinergic drug is most likely being prescribed?

explanation.summary: Scopolamine, a transdermal-patch anticholinergic, is used for motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states scopolamine (hyoscine) is usually formulated as a transdermal patch to treat motion sickness and postsurgical nausea, and that the patches are not for continuous use and should be replaced after 72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is used for bradycardia, reducing secretions, and as a poisoning antidote, not as a motion-sickness patch.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats urinary urge incontinence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic drop used to dilate the pupil.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with COPD is prescribed an inhaled anticholinergic to add to his beta-agonist and inhaled corticosteroid. By blocking M3 receptors in the airways, this drug relieves his symptoms. Which effect on the airways is responsible for the benefit?

explanation.summary: Inhaled anticholinergics such as ipratropium cause bronchodilation and reduce mucus secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that M3 receptors in the lungs can cause bronchoconstriction; blocking them with ipratropium or tiotropium reduces mucus secretions and bronchoconstriction, lowering airway resistance and allowing easier breathing in asthma and COPD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoconstriction and increased secretions are the parasympathetic effects that anticholinergics oppose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The benefit comes from bronchodilation and decreased secretions, not increased ciliary clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surfactant production is not a described mechanism of these drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes the effect to airway smooth muscle and secretions, not pulmonary vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a sudden, frequent urge to urinate with occasional involuntary leakage, and urodynamic testing shows detrusor overactivity. She is started on oxybutynin. What is the mechanism by which this drug relieves her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors in the bladder neck and trigone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking muscarinic receptors to slow detrusor contractions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing urine production through a renal diuretic effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relaxing the internal urethral sphincter to ease voiding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulating detrusor muscle contraction to empty the bladder

explanation.summary: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic that slows detrusor contractions to control urge incontinence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes oxybutynin as the prototypical anticholinergic for urinary incontinence (overactive bladder); by blocking M3 receptors it slows bladder detrusor contractions, helping patients control urine output.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxybutynin is antimuscarinic, not an alpha-adrenergic blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The drug does not increase urine production; it reduces involuntary bladder contractions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics reduce detrusor overactivity; they do not work by relaxing the urethral sphincter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating detrusor contraction would worsen urgency and leakage.

questions.stem: An ophthalmologist needs to dilate a patient's pupil to examine the retina during a funduscopic exam. Which of the following anticholinergic agents, administered as an eye drop, is most appropriate for producing mydriasis?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic drops such as tropicamide (or atropine) dilate the pupil for eye exams.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that atropine and tropicamide drops are used to dilate the pupil for ophthalmoscopic exams; the mydriasis helps with retinal and pupillary examination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycopyrrolate does not penetrate well and is not described as an ophthalmic mydriatic agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats overactive bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine is used as a transdermal patch for motion sickness, not as an ophthalmic dilating drop.

questions.stem: A toxicology instructor teaches the classic anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic. A poisoned patient who is described as 'mad as a hatter' is exhibiting which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased secretions, dry mouth, and thirst

explanation.summary: 'Mad as a hatter' refers to the CNS effects of anticholinergic toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick maps 'mad as a hatter' to central nervous system effects such as drowsiness, hallucinations, and coma, which result from central muscarinic blockade in agents that penetrate the CNS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dry mouth and decreased secretions correspond to 'dry as a bone'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flushed skin corresponds to 'red as a beet'.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mydriasis and blurred vision correspond to 'blind as a bat'.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tachycardia (and overheating) corresponds to 'hot as a hare'.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with severe lower abdominal pain and states he has not urinated in several days. He has no prior urinary problems and is generally healthy but recently began an over-the-counter allergy medicine for a runny nose. Examination reveals a markedly distended bladder requiring catheterization. Which property of his allergy medication best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains diphenhydramine with anticholinergic properties

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a direct cholinergic agonist that stimulates the detrusor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a diuretic that overfilled the bladder

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist that relaxes the bladder neck

explanation.summary: OTC diphenhydramine has anticholinergic properties that can cause urinary retention, especially in the elderly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case describes exactly this scenario: the allergy medicine contains diphenhydramine, an antihistamine with anticholinergic properties. By blocking muscarinic receptors it decreases detrusor contraction and causes urinary retention, a particular risk in elderly patients who also face confusion, constipation, and falls.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A cholinergic agonist would promote urination, not cause retention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A diuretic would increase urine output; the problem was inability to void due to anticholinergic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor increases acetylcholine and cholinergic activity, opposite to what caused retention.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-blockade at the bladder neck would ease urine flow, not cause retention.

questions.stem: A patient who took a large amount of an anticholinergic agent is brought to the emergency department. On the anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic, the finding 'dry as a bone' reflects which underlying mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of cardiac vagal tone at M2 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cutaneous vasodilation in the skin vasculature

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased gut motility with delayed transit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pupillary dilation from iris sphincter blockade

explanation.summary: 'Dry as a bone' reflects inhibition of secretions, producing dry mouth, dry eyes, and decreased sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick attributes 'dry as a bone' to the general inhibition of secretions in mucous membranes and skin, giving dry mouth, dry eyes, and reduced sweating from muscarinic blockade of exocrine glands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blockade of cardiac vagal tone produces tachycardia ('hot as a hare').
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cutaneous flushing corresponds to 'red as a beet'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased gut motility contributes to 'full as a flask' (retention/constipation).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pupillary dilation corresponds to 'blind as a bat'.

questions.stem: A farm worker is brought in after exposure to an organophosphate insecticide, with copious secretions, bradycardia, and pinpoint pupils. Which anticholinergic drug is the appropriate antidote for this acetylcholine-excess (muscarinic) toxicity?

explanation.summary: Atropine is the antidote for acetylcholine toxicity, such as organophosphate or muscarine poisoning.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states atropine is an antidote for acetylcholine toxicity, including poisoning by organophosphates or muscarine-containing wild mushrooms. By competitively blocking muscarinic receptors, it reverses the excess-cholinergic secretions, bradycardia, and miosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin is a bladder-selective agent for overactive bladder, not a poisoning antidote.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine is used for motion sickness, not as the antidote of choice for cholinergic crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic drop for pupil dilation.

questions.stem: A student is asked to predict adverse effects of anticholinergic drugs from their receptor actions. Which of the following is a likely adverse effect of an anticholinergic agent?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics decrease GI motility, which can lead to constipation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's review question confirms constipation as a correct answer: anticholinergics inhibit gut smooth muscle contraction and decrease motility, which can cause constipation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They cause tachycardia by blocking vagal tone, not bradycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They decrease, not increase, GI motility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics decrease secretions, causing dry mouth, not increased salivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They cause mydriasis (dilation), not miosis.

questions.stem: A neurologist notes that some antimuscarinic drugs are useful for CNS diseases while others are not, depending on how well they penetrate the brain. Which of the following best explains why ipratropium and glycopyrrolate are NOT useful in treating Parkinson disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are direct dopamine receptor antagonists in the striatum

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are rapidly metabolized in the gut wall before they are absorbed

choices.label: C
choices.text: They block nicotinic rather than muscarinic receptors in the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: They do not adequately cross into the central nervous system

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate rather than block muscarinic receptors centrally

explanation.summary: CNS penetration varies among antimuscarinics; poorly penetrating agents cannot treat central diseases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that muscarinic antagonists have variable CNS penetration. Certain agents (e.g., benztropine, atropine) carry greater CNS effects, whereas ipratropium and glycopyrrolate do not penetrate the CNS well and therefore are not useful in treating CNS diseases such as Parkinson disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are antimuscarinics, not dopamine antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the difference to CNS penetration, not to pre-absorption metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These drugs are muscarinic antagonists; the issue is CNS penetration, not a switch to nicotinic blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They block, rather than stimulate, muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: A microbiology laboratory incubates a standardized suspension of a patient's isolate with a series of tubes containing rising amounts of an antibiotic. After about a day, the technician records the lowest drug concentration at which the tube stays clear. Which of the following does this value represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clinical breakpoint for the organism-drug pair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minimum bactericidal concentration of the drug

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minimum inhibitory concentration of the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peak serum concentration needed for efficacy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Post-antibiotic effect threshold of the drug

explanation.summary: The MIC is the lowest antibiotic concentration with no visible bacterial growth after incubation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The MIC is determined by mixing a standard concentration of the organism with increasing antibiotic concentrations and incubating for about a day. Cloudiness indicates growth, and the lowest concentration with no visible growth is the MIC, the measurement used clinically to determine susceptibility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The breakpoint is a published cutoff MIC used to call an isolate susceptible; it is not read off the patient's tubes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The MBC requires showing a 99.9% reduction in the original colony count, not just a clear tube.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peak concentration is a patient pharmacokinetic value, not a laboratory dilution result.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The post-antibiotic effect describes suppressed growth after levels fall in vivo; it is not measured by the lowest clear tube.

questions.stem: In a dilution study, a new drug has an MIC of 0.5 μg/mL against a patient's isolate, and subculture first shows a 99.9% drop in the original colony count at 1 μg/mL. Which of the following best classifies the drug against this isolate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bactericidal, since the MBC/MIC ratio is 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bactericidal, since the MIC is under 1 μg/mL

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bacteriostatic, since the MBC is above the MIC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bacteriostatic, since the MBC/MIC ratio is 2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Indeterminate, since the MBC is rarely measured

explanation.summary: An MBC/MIC ratio below 4 classifies an agent as bactericidal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The MBC is the concentration giving a 99.9% reduction in the original colony count, here 1 μg/mL. Dividing by the MIC of 0.5 μg/mL gives a ratio of 2. Per the lecture, MBC/MIC < 4 is bactericidal and > 4 is bacteriostatic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The absolute MIC does not determine the classification; only the MBC/MIC comparison does.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The MBC is always at least the MIC; classification depends on the size of the ratio, and a ratio of 2 is bactericidal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An MBC/MIC ratio below 4 defines bactericidal, not bacteriostatic, activity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MBC is rarely obtained clinically, but here it was measured, so the ratio can be calculated.

questions.stem: An antibacterial agent has an MIC of 0.25 μg/mL and an MBC of 8 μg/mL against a patient's isolate. It is used to treat an uncomplicated infection in an otherwise healthy, immunocompetent adult, who recovers fully. Which of the following best explains how this agent achieved cure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It halted growth so host defenses could clear it

choices.label: B
choices.text: It killed the organism directly as its primary action

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lowered the organism's MIC over repeated doses

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reached peak levels that eradicated the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: It sustained killing through a post-antibiotic effect

explanation.summary: Bacteriostatic agents (MBC/MIC > 4) halt growth so that an immunocompetent host can clear the organism.
explanation.whyCorrect: The MBC/MIC ratio is 8/0.25 = 32, so the agent is bacteriostatic. Bacteriostatic agents halt bacterial growth and replication, and the immunocompetent host then clears the organism, which makes these agents as effective as bactericidal ones for most infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An MBC/MIC ratio of 32 is well above 4, so killing is not this agent's primary action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeated dosing does not lower an isolate's MIC; the MIC is a property measured in the laboratory.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eradication by peak concentrations describes concentration-dependent killing, not an agent whose MBC far exceeds its MIC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The post-antibiotic effect is described for aminoglycosides; it does not explain cure by an agent with a ratio of 32.

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacist recommends giving a β-lactam antibiotic as a prolonged infusion rather than a short bolus, keeping the same daily amount. Which pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic index is this strategy designed to optimize?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Length of the post-antibiotic effect after a dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peak concentration achieved relative to the MIC

choices.label: C
choices.text: Percentage of the dosing interval above the MIC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ratio of the MBC to the MIC for the isolate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Total drug exposure over time relative to the MIC

explanation.summary: β-Lactams are time-dependent: efficacy tracks %T>MIC, which prolonged infusion or more frequent dosing increases.
explanation.whyCorrect: For β-lactams, efficacy is associated with the percentage of the dosing interval during which the drug concentration remains above the MIC. More frequent dosing or prolonged infusion increases this time above the MIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The post-antibiotic effect is a feature of aminoglycosides, not the target of β-lactam infusion strategies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cmax/MIC is the index for aminoglycosides; a prolonged infusion lowers rather than raises the peak.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MBC/MIC classifies bacteriostatic versus bactericidal activity; it is not a dosing target.
whyWrongByChoice.E: AUC/MIC is the index for vancomycin and fluoroquinolones, not β-lactams.

questions.stem: A patient with a serious infection is started on an aminoglycoside. The team chooses one large dose every 24 hours instead of smaller doses every 8 hours, even though serum levels fall well below the MIC late in each interval. Which pair of properties best justifies this regimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exposure-driven killing and an MBC/MIC ratio above 4

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peak-to-MIC driven killing and a post-antibiotic effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peak-to-MIC driven killing and an MBC/MIC ratio above 4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Time-above-MIC driven killing and a post-antibiotic effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Time-above-MIC driven killing and bacteriostatic action

explanation.summary: Aminoglycosides are concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC) and have a post-antibiotic effect, favoring large, less frequent doses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aminoglycoside efficacy is associated with peak concentration relative to the MIC, so relatively larger, less frequent doses maximize the peak. They also show a post-antibiotic effect: bacterial growth remains suppressed for a period after concentrations fall, so low late-interval levels are tolerated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AUC/MIC governs vancomycin and fluoroquinolones, and a ratio above 4 indicates bacteriostatic action, neither of which justifies the regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cmax/MIC is correct, but a ratio above 4 does not explain why low trough levels are tolerated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aminoglycosides are not time-dependent; time-above-MIC dependence would argue against long intervals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Time-above-MIC dependence would favor frequent dosing, the opposite of this regimen.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is receiving intravenous vancomycin for a bloodstream infection. The clinical pharmacist monitors his drug levels to make sure therapy is likely to succeed. Which pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic index best predicts the efficacy of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Area under the curve relative to the MIC

choices.label: B
choices.text: MBC-to-MIC ratio of the infecting isolate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peak concentration relative to the MIC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Time spent above the MIC per interval

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trough concentration relative to the MBC

explanation.summary: Vancomycin efficacy is best predicted by AUC/MIC (exposure-dependent activity).
explanation.whyCorrect: Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones are the representative exposure-dependent drugs: efficacy is associated with total drug exposure over time (AUC) relative to the MIC.

whyWrongByChoice.B: MBC/MIC classifies bacteriostatic versus bactericidal activity rather than predicting dosing efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cmax/MIC predicts efficacy for aminoglycosides, not vancomycin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: %T>MIC predicts efficacy for β-lactams, not vancomycin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lecture does not describe a trough/MBC index; MBC is rarely used clinically.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has a deep wound infection that is improving more slowly than expected. The susceptibility report classifies his isolate as 'intermediate' to the agent he is receiving. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antibiogram shows falling local susceptibility

choices.label: B
choices.text: The drug halts growth but cannot kill this isolate

choices.label: C
choices.text: The MBC/MIC ratio shows bacteriostatic drug action

choices.label: D
choices.text: The MIC nears ordinarily achievable drug levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: The organism is resistant and the drug cannot work

explanation.summary: An intermediate result means the MIC approaches ordinarily achievable drug concentrations and response is less predictable; it is not resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The lecture defines intermediate as an MIC approaching ordinarily achievable drug concentrations, a response that may be less predictable than for a susceptible isolate, or a result within a buffer range for testing variability. It is not synonymous with resistance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The report describes this patient's isolate; an antibiogram is a separate population-level summary.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Growth inhibition versus killing is a bacteriostatic/bactericidal distinction, not what the intermediate category reports.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Susceptibility categories are based on the MIC relative to breakpoints, not on the MBC/MIC ratio.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An intermediate result is not synonymous with resistance.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is admitted with suspected urosepsis. Blood and urine cultures are drawn, but organism identification and testing will not be available for 2 days. Which of the following best guides the initial choice of antibiotic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her pending culture and susceptibility report

choices.label: B
choices.text: MBC testing of her isolate in a research lab

choices.label: C
choices.text: National breakpoint tables for each drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug with the lowest MIC for the organism

choices.label: E
choices.text: The hospital's antibiogram of local isolates

explanation.summary: Antibiograms guide empiric therapy before patient-specific culture and susceptibility results are available.
explanation.whyCorrect: An antibiogram summarizes the percentage of isolates within a facility or community that were susceptible to specific antibiotics over a defined period. Clinicians use it to select empiric therapy before the patient's own culture and susceptibility results return.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This report will guide definitive therapy, but it is not yet available for the empiric choice.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MBC data are hard to obtain, are rarely acquired outside research, and would not be available in time.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breakpoints define susceptibility cutoffs; they do not show which drugs local organisms are likely susceptible to.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lowest MIC does not identify the best drug, and her organism's MICs are not yet known.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has acute cystitis. Testing of her isolate reports an MIC of 0.06 μg/mL for drug X and 0.5 μg/mL for drug Y. Drug X reaches only low levels in the urine, whereas drug Y is concentrated in the bladder. Both are classified as susceptible. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drug X is preferable owing to its eightfold lower MIC

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug X is preferable owing to its likely bactericidal action

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drug Y is preferable owing to its presumably higher MBC

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug Y may be preferable owing to where it distributes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neither drug is usable until each MBC is measured

explanation.summary: The lowest MIC does not make a drug the best choice; drug concentration at the infection site matters.
explanation.whyCorrect: Different antibiotics achieve different concentrations at different body sites (for example, CNS versus bladder), so MICs for a single organism should not be compared across drugs. A drug that concentrates at the site of infection may be the better choice despite a higher MIC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MICs should not be compared across drugs; the lowest MIC does not make a drug the best choice.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A low MIC alone does not establish bactericidal activity; that needs the MBC/MIC comparison.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A higher MBC would not make a drug preferable, and no MBC data are given.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MBC is rarely needed clinically; both drugs are already reported susceptible.

questions.stem: Each of the following patients is otherwise healthy and has an infection for which both a bacteriostatic and a bactericidal agent are active. In which patient is a bactericidal agent most clearly preferred?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 34-year-old man with acute bacterial sinusitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 45-year-old woman with a superficial abscess

explanation.summary: Bactericidal drugs are preferred for certain infections such as endocarditis and meningitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although outcomes with bacteriostatic and bactericidal drugs are similar for most infections, bactericidal drugs are preferred for infections like endocarditis and meningitis, where the anatomic location limits how effectively the immune system can clear the organism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An uncomplicated infection in an immunocompetent host is cleared well with a bacteriostatic agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: For most infections, outcomes with appropriate bacteriostatic and bactericidal drugs are similar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is not one of the infections in which bactericidal drugs are preferred; outcomes are generally similar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A superficial infection in a healthy host does not call for a bactericidal agent specifically.

questions.stem: For a given organism and antibiotic, a national organization publishes a cutoff MIC at or below which an isolate is reported as susceptible. What is this cutoff called?

explanation.summary: The breakpoint is the published MIC cutoff that defines susceptibility for each organism-antibiotic pair.
explanation.whyCorrect: For each organism-antibiotic pair there is a particular cutoff MIC considered susceptible. This MIC is the breakpoint, which is closely monitored and published by a national organization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An antibiogram reports the percentage of local isolates susceptible; it does not set the cutoff.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The MBC is the concentration giving 99.9% killing, not a published susceptibility cutoff.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cmax/MIC is a PK/PD index predicting aminoglycoside efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The post-antibiotic effect describes suppressed growth after drug levels fall.

questions.stem: Two regimens of the same β-lactam, each delivering the same total daily amount, are compared against an isolate with an MIC of 2 μg/mL. Regimen 1 gives one large dose every 24 hours: its peak is four times higher, but levels exceed 2 μg/mL for only 6 hours. Regimen 2 gives smaller doses every 6 hours, and levels exceed 2 μg/mL for 18 hours of each day. Which statement best predicts their relative efficacy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are equal, owing to similar total drug exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regimen 1, owing to a longer post-antibiotic effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regimen 1, owing to its higher peak-to-MIC ratio

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regimen 2, owing to a lower MBC-to-MIC ratio

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regimen 2, owing to longer time spent above the MIC

explanation.summary: For time-dependent β-lactams, the regimen that keeps levels above the MIC longest is predicted to work best.
explanation.whyCorrect: β-Lactams show time-dependent activity: efficacy is associated with %T>MIC. Regimen 2 keeps concentrations above the MIC for 75% of the day versus 25% for regimen 1, so it is predicted to be more effective despite its lower peak.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AUC/MIC governs vancomycin and fluoroquinolones; for β-lactams, the time above MIC matters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The post-antibiotic effect is described for aminoglycosides and does not rescue a β-lactam regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peak/MIC predicts aminoglycoside efficacy, not β-lactam efficacy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dosing schedule does not change the MBC/MIC ratio, which is a laboratory property of drug and isolate.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with streptococcal pharyngitis is treated with penicillin V. Which of the following molecular actions accounts for the drug's antibacterial effect?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pore formation in the cytoplasmic membrane

explanation.summary: β-lactams covalently bind penicillin-binding proteins such as transpeptidases and block the final cross-linking step of peptidoglycan synthesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillin V is a β-lactam. β-lactams covalently bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), including transpeptidases, and inhibit the final cross-linking step of peptidoglycan synthesis. The weakened wall leads to osmotic lysis, so the effect is bactericidal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribosomal binding is the mechanism of protein-synthesis inhibitors, not of β-lactams.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Topoisomerase (DNA gyrase) inhibition belongs to other antibacterial classes, not penicillins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Membrane disruption is not how β-lactams act; they target cell-wall synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autolysin activation, not suppression, may add to the cell-wall degradation that β-lactams cause.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a large thigh abscess. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus that is resistant to methicillin and nafcillin, and adding a β-lactamase inhibitor to a penicillin does not restore activity. Which of the following best explains this isolate's resistance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydrolysis of the drugs by staphylococcal penicillinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of outer-membrane porins that admit the drugs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overproduction of autolysins that degrade the wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal dehydropeptidase I metabolism of the drugs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Target proteins with reduced affinity for the drugs

explanation.summary: Methicillin-resistant staphylococci resist β-lactams through altered PBPs, which β-lactamase inhibitors cannot overcome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Structural changes in penicillin-binding proteins reduce the drug's affinity for its target. This is the major mechanism of β-lactam resistance in methicillin-resistant staphylococci. Because no enzyme is destroying the drug, adding clavulanate, sulbactam, or tazobactam does not help.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nafcillin is stable against staphylococcal penicillinase, and an inhibitor would counter a susceptible β-lactamase; neither fits this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Porin changes reduce penetration in gram-negative bacteria; S. aureus is gram-positive and lacks an outer membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autolysin activation contributes to β-lactam killing; it is not a resistance mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dehydropeptidase I is a human renal enzyme that metabolizes imipenem; it is not a bacterial resistance mechanism.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with bacterial sinusitis does not improve on amoxicillin. Her isolate produces an enzyme that opens the four-membered ring of the drug. She is switched to amoxicillin/clavulanate and recovers. Which of the following is the role of clavulanate in this regimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking renal tubular secretion of the partner

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhancing porin entry of the partner into cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restoring PBP affinity for the partner drug

explanation.summary: Clavulanate, sulbactam, and tazobactam inhibit certain β-lactamases and protect a coadministered penicillin from hydrolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The isolate's enzyme is a β-lactamase that hydrolyzes the β-lactam ring and inactivates amoxicillin. Clavulanate inhibits certain β-lactamases, protecting the partner penicillin so that amoxicillin can reach and bind its PBPs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking tubular secretion is the action of probenecid, which raises penicillin serum levels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clavulanate does not improve penetration; inhibitors do not overcome decreased penetration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibiting renal dehydropeptidase I is the role of cilastatin, paired with imipenem.
whyWrongByChoice.D: β-lactamase inhibitors do not overcome resistance caused by altered PBPs.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man receiving maintenance hemodialysis needs a penicillin. His pharmacist notes that most penicillins are excreted largely unchanged in the urine. Which of the following penicillins relies substantially on hepatic and biliary elimination instead?

explanation.summary: Nafcillin is the important penicillin exception whose clearance depends substantially on hepatic and biliary elimination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most penicillins and carbapenems are eliminated primarily by the kidneys and need dose adjustment in renal impairment. Nafcillin, a β-lactamase-resistant (antistaphylococcal) penicillin, is mainly excreted in the bile, with hepatic and biliary elimination contributing substantially to its clearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amoxicillin, like most penicillins, is eliminated primarily by the kidneys.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penicillin G is eliminated primarily by the kidneys and requires renal dose adjustment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penicillin V is eliminated mainly by the kidneys.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Piperacillin is eliminated mainly by the kidneys and needs adjustment in renal impairment.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with a polymicrobial intra-abdominal infection is treated with imipenem coformulated with cilastatin. The cilastatin component works by inhibiting which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dehydropeptidase I in the proximal tubule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Organic anion secretion in the renal tubule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transpeptidase PBPs in the bacterial wall

explanation.summary: Cilastatin inhibits renal dehydropeptidase I, preventing renal metabolism of imipenem.
explanation.whyCorrect: Imipenem is metabolized in the kidneys by dehydropeptidase I, an enzyme in the proximal tubular brush border. Cilastatin inhibits this enzyme, limiting renal metabolism of imipenem and allowing adequate antibacterial concentrations of imipenem in the urine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cilastatin does not act on hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes; its target is a renal brush-border enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of tubular secretion describes probenecid, not cilastatin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cilastatin is not a β-lactamase inhibitor; clavulanate, sulbactam, and tazobactam play that role.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PBPs are the target of imipenem itself; cilastatin has no independent antibacterial activity.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man in the intensive care unit develops ventilator-associated pneumonia. Sputum culture grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The team is choosing among several agents from the same class. Which of the following would be expected to lack activity against this organism?

explanation.summary: Ertapenem is the carbapenem that lacks activity against P. aeruginosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbapenems have broad activity, and imipenem/cilastatin, meropenem, and doripenem cover susceptible P. aeruginosa. Ertapenem has broad activity but lacks activity against P. aeruginosa, so it would be the wrong choice here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Doripenem has broad activity that includes susceptible P. aeruginosa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imipenem/cilastatin has broad activity that includes susceptible P. aeruginosa.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meropenem has broad activity that includes susceptible P. aeruginosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Meropenem/vaborbactam contains meropenem, which covers susceptible P. aeruginosa.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with epilepsy has been seizure-free for years on valproic acid. She is hospitalized for pyelonephritis caused by an ESBL-producing Escherichia coli and started on meropenem. Two days later she has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Her kidney function is normal. Which of the following most likely precipitated the seizure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of meropenem from poor clearance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marked fall in her serum anticonvulsant level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of toxins from dying gram-negatives

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rise in her anticonvulsant level to toxicity

explanation.summary: Carbapenems can markedly reduce serum valproate concentrations, causing breakthrough seizures; concomitant use should generally be avoided.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbapenems interact with valproic acid by markedly reducing serum valproate concentrations, which increases the risk of breakthrough seizures. With normal kidney function, drug accumulation is unlikely, so loss of seizure control from low valproate is the best explanation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Accumulation from impaired renal elimination raises seizure risk, but her kidney function is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgE- or IgG-mediated hypersensitivity does not explain a seizure in a patient whose seizures were previously controlled.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A reaction to products of dying organisms describes the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after treating spirochetes, not this.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carbapenems decrease, rather than increase, serum valproate concentrations.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease is treated for a hospital-acquired infection with imipenem/cilastatin at standard doses, without adjustment. On day 3 he has a generalized seizure. He takes no other medications. Which of the following best explains the seizure?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Breakthrough from a fall in serum valproate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cilastatin inhibition of hepatic drug clearance

explanation.summary: Imipenem/cilastatin is renally eliminated; accumulation in renal impairment lowers the seizure threshold.
explanation.whyCorrect: Imipenem/cilastatin is eliminated primarily by the kidneys and requires dose adjustment in renal impairment. Without adjustment the drug accumulates, increasing the risk of central nervous system effects including seizures. The risk of seizures is greatest with imipenem/cilastatin among the carbapenems.

whyWrongByChoice.B: He takes no other medications, so a carbapenem-valproate interaction cannot apply.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cilastatin acts on renal dehydropeptidase I, not on hepatic clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nothing in the presentation suggests anaphylaxis, such as urticaria, bronchospasm, or hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C. difficile infection causes diarrhea and colitis, not seizures.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl has sore throat, fever, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. She is given amoxicillin and, several days later, develops a generalized maculopapular rash. A heterophile antibody test is positive. Which of the following best describes this rash?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rash tied to Epstein-Barr virus infection

explanation.summary: Ampicillin and amoxicillin can cause a generalized maculopapular rash in infectious mononucleosis that is not necessarily an IgE-mediated allergy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ampicillin and amoxicillin (aminopenicillins) can cause a generalized maculopapular rash, particularly in patients with Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis. A positive heterophile test confirms mononucleosis. This reaction is not necessarily an IgE-mediated allergy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The aminopenicillin rash in mononucleosis is not necessarily an IgE-mediated allergy, and she has no anaphylactic features.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum sickness includes fever, arthralgias, and lymphadenopathy 1-3 weeks after exposure; this rash has a specific association with mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction follows treatment of spirochetal infections such as syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A positive heterophile test points to infectious mononucleosis, not a streptococcal toxin rash.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is on day 12 of high-dose intravenous penicillin for a deep soft-tissue infection. He develops fever and a diffuse rash. Serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows hematuria; blood eosinophils are increased. Which of the following immune mechanisms underlies this complication?

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgG binding to coated red cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of toxins from dying microbes

explanation.summary: Penicillin-associated acute interstitial nephritis is a Type IV (T-cell-mediated, delayed) hypersensitivity reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fever, rash, eosinophilia, hematuria, and impaired kidney function during penicillin therapy indicate acute interstitial nephritis. Type IV delayed hypersensitivity, which is T-cell-mediated, can cause delayed cutaneous eruptions or acute interstitial nephritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgE-mediated reactions occur within minutes to hours and cause urticaria, bronchospasm, or anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgG against penicillin bound to red cells causes Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia, not kidney injury with eosinophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immune-complex reactions produce serum sickness with arthralgias and lymphadenopathy; interstitial nephritis is classified as a T-cell-mediated reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Release of microbial products occurs in the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within 24 hours of treating spirochetes.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with hospital-acquired pneumonia is started on piperacillin/tazobactam. To which penicillin subgroup does piperacillin belong?

explanation.summary: Penicillins are classified as natural, antistaphylococcal, aminopenicillin, or antipseudomonal agents; piperacillin is antipseudomonal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penicillins are classified by structure, spectrum, and β-lactamase stability into natural, antistaphylococcal, aminopenicillin, and antipseudomonal groups. Piperacillin is an antipseudomonal penicillin and, combined with tazobactam, sits at the broad end of the penicillin spectrum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aminopenicillins are ampicillin and amoxicillin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nafcillin is the antistaphylococcal penicillin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbapenems are a separate β-lactam class with a different ring structure, not a penicillin subgroup.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Natural penicillins include penicillin G and penicillin V.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman is on day 6 of amoxicillin for a respiratory infection. She develops frequent watery diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain, and leukocytosis. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Antibacterial therapy can disrupt the colonic microbiota and permit overgrowth of toxigenic Clostridioides difficile.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like other antibacterial drugs, penicillins can disrupt the normal colonic microbiota, permitting overgrowth of toxigenic Clostridioides difficile. The resulting diarrhea ranges from mild to severe pseudomembranous colitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is not the organism associated with antibiotic-related disruption of the colonic microbiota.
whyWrongByChoice.C: P. aeruginosa is not the cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. aureus is not the organism linked to antibiotic-associated colitis in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a respiratory pathogen, not a cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
